analysis.one_liner: Eases the burden of proof for older workers suing over age discrimination, and for disability and retaliation claims.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with a bipartisan cosponsor, has sat in the Senate labor committee with no hearing, no vote, and no further action since May 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: After a 2009 Supreme Court ruling, workers who claim they were pushed out because of their age must prove age was the deciding cause, not just one reason — a much harder standard. This bill would restore the easier "motivating factor" test: an older worker wins by showing age was one reason an employer acted, even if other reasons were also involved. It applies the same standard to disability discrimination and anti-retaliation claims under several federal laws, and applies to cases already in court. If an employer proves it would have made the same decision anyway, the worker can get attorney's fees and a court order declaring the practice unlawful, but no money damages.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers age 40 and over who are demoted, fired, or passed over and believe age was part of the reason, along with workers with disabilities and employees who face retaliation for asserting their rights. Under current law they must prove the protected trait was the sole decisive cause, which many can't do; this bill would let them win by showing it was one motivating factor.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Older workers and workers with disabilities

how_it_helps.text: Restores the "motivating factor" standard under the Age Discrimination in Employment Act: a worker establishes a violation by showing age was a motivating factor, even if other factors also motivated the employer's decision, and is not required to show age was the sole cause.
Allows a complaining party to rely on any type or form of admissible evidence, needing only enough evidence for a reasonable jury to find a violation occurred.

Applies the same motivating-factor standard and evidence rules to disability discrimination claims under the Americans with Disabilities Act, to Title VII race/sex/religion/national-origin and retaliation claims, and to federal employees under the Rehabilitation Act and related statutes.
Applies to all claims pending on or after the date of enactment, so workers with cases already in court would benefit.

If the employer proves it would have taken the same action without the unlawful motive, the court may still grant declaratory relief, injunctive relief, and attorney's fees, but no damages or reinstatement — a compromise aimed at deterring discrimination without exposing employers to full liability.

analysis.who_pays: Employers, who would face discrimination lawsuits that are easier to get to a jury and easier to win, and would bear attorney's fees and settlement costs in cases where a mixed motive is shown. Businesses with older workforces would feel this most in hiring, layoffs, and promotion decisions.

drawbacks.text: The motivating-factor standard sweeps in situations where age played only a small part, so employers can face findings of discrimination for decisions that would have come out the same way; the bill limits such cases to fees and court orders with no damages, but the litigation cost and reputational harm remain.

Making the standard apply to all claims pending on or after enactment changes the rules midstream for lawsuits already filed, which raises fairness and predictability objections for employers and courts.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to older workers is real and targeted: the Supreme Court's 2009 shift to a "but-for" standard made age cases unusually hard to win, and this bill would return to the rule workers had before, while capping employer exposure in same-decision cases to fees and orders rather than damages. The cost is higher litigation and settlement expense for employers, some of which will be cases where age was a minor factor. The bill is a deliberate compromise, not a one-sided expansion of liability.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate labor committee in May 2025, and has had no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote since.

narrative.text: Sen. Tammy Baldwin introduced the bill on May 20, 2025, joined by Sens. Chuck Grassley (R) and Sheldon Whitehouse (D).
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions, where it remains.
No further action — no hearing, committee vote, or floor vote — appears in the action history.
The bill text would restore the motivating-factor standard for age, disability, and retaliation claims, applying to all claims pending on or after enactment.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers and business groups are better off for now: with no committee action, the current harder-to-win standard for age discrimination claims stays in place, and employers avoid the added litigation exposure the bill would create.

for.name: Sen. Tammy Baldwin
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to restore the motivating-factor standard for age discrimination and related claims.

for.name: Sen. Chuck Grassley
for.what_they_did: Original cosponsor, giving the bill bipartisan sponsorship.

against.name: Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral in May 2025 and has taken no action — no hearing or markup — as of the latest action history.

against.name: Senate Republican leadership
against.role: Controls the Senate floor calendar in the 119th Congress
against.what_they_did: Has not brought the bill to the floor; nothing reaches a vote without leadership deciding to schedule it.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's three original sponsors split across parties — one Republican and two Democrats — so there is no party split to judge from a roll call; no vote has occurred.

industries.industry: Employers (businesses with workforces covered by federal anti-discrimination law)
industries.note: The bill would make age, disability, and retaliation claims easier to win, adding litigation and settlement costs for employers. Its interest in defeating the bill runs against older workers' ability to challenge discriminatory firings and layoffs.
Easier-to-prove claims with attorney's-fee provisions mean more viable cases for lawyers representing workers. In this bill that interest runs alongside older workers' interests.

analysis.trajectory: With only two cosponsors and no committee action more than a year into the session, the bill is unlikely to get a standalone vote. Its realistic path is being folded into a broader workforce or retirement package if one moves; otherwise it will die in committee at the end of the Congress.
